cards.title: Zero Trust — Never Trust, Always Verify
cards.teaser: Zero Trust is not a product — it is a security philosophy that abandons the concept of a trusted internal network. Every request, from every source, must be authenticated, authorized, and continuously re-evaluated as if the network is already compromised.

runs.text: The traditional security model assumed that anything inside the corporate network perimeter was safe. Once an employee (or attacker) was inside the firewall, lateral movement was relatively free. This model broke down with mobile work, cloud adoption, and sophisticated attackers who routinely breach the perimeter.
Zero Trust replaces the perimeter model with a single axiom:

items.text: Never trust, always verify
— no user, device, or network segment is inherently trusted. Every access request must be verified against identity, device posture, context, and policy before being granted.
Assume breach
— design controls as if the attacker is already inside. Minimize blast radius through least-privilege access and micro-segmentation.
Least privilege
— grant the minimum permissions needed for the task, for the minimum time required. No standing access to sensitive resources.

runs.text: The term was coined by John Kindervag at Forrester Research in 2010, but its most influential practical realization came from Google's BeyondCorp program, which began the same year. NIST SP 800-207 (2020) provides the authoritative federal definition.

Zero Trust is architecture, not a product category. Vendors sell "Zero Trust solutions" but buying a product does not make you Zero Trust. ZTA is a set of principles applied across people, process, and technology.

Zero Trust means you stop assuming that being inside the network makes you trustworthy. Every request gets checked — who you are, what device you're on, what you need — before you get in. There is no safe zone.

cards.title: BeyondCorp — Google's Zero Trust Blueprint
cards.teaser: BeyondCorp, described in a series of Google papers beginning in 2014, moved all Google employee access off the VPN and onto the open internet — authenticated purely by device certificate and user identity. It became the de facto reference implementation of Zero Trust.

runs.text: Google published the foundational BeyondCorp paper — "BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security" — in the USENIX ;login: magazine in 2014. The series extended through 2018 covering design, migration, and lessons learned.
The core shift BeyondCorp made:

items.text: From VPN to the open internet.
Employees access internal applications over the public internet, not through a VPN tunnel. The network location (inside or outside the office) grants zero privileges.
Device inventory as access control.

Every managed device receives a device certificate issued by Google. Access decisions check whether the requesting device is in the managed device inventory and meets current security posture requirements.
Access proxy, not network access.
Users authenticate to an access proxy in front of each application. The proxy enforces access policy. Users never get broad network access — only application-level access to specific resources.
Context-aware authorization.

Authorization decisions incorporate user identity, group membership, device certificate, device posture (patch level, disk encryption status), and request context (time, location, sensitivity of resource).

runs.text: The BeyondCorp model demonstrated at Google's scale (tens of thousands of employees) that VPN-less enterprise access was practical. It proved that the network perimeter is not a necessary security primitive — identity and device posture can replace it.
The full BeyondCorp paper series is available at research.google/pubs. The 2014 foundational paper (Ward and Beyer) and the 2017 design paper (Peck et al.) are the highest-value reads for architects.

BeyondCorp is Google's proof of concept for Zero Trust: they killed the VPN and made every employee authenticate through a secure proxy on the open internet, using their identity and device certificate — not their network location — to get access.

cards.title: ZTA Principles — NIST SP 800-207
cards.teaser: NIST SP 800-207 (2020) codified Zero Trust Architecture as a federal standard. Its three core tenets — verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach — give organizations a vendor-neutral framework for designing ZTA.

runs.text: NIST Special Publication 800-207, "Zero Trust Architecture," was published in August 2020. It defines ZTA, describes its components, and gives deployment models. The three tenets that anchor the document:

items.text: Verify explicitly.

Always authenticate and authorize based on all available data points: user identity, location, device health, service or workload, data classification, and anomalies. Do not grant access based on network location alone.
Use least privileged access.
Limit user access with just-in-time (JIT) and just-enough-access (JEA). Apply adaptive policies and data protection. Minimize lateral movement opportunities.
Assume breach.

Minimize blast radius. Segment access. Encrypt all communications end-to-end. Maintain full telemetry to detect and respond to anomalies. Design as if an attacker already has persistent access somewhere in the environment.

runs.text: NIST 800-207 also defines three ZTA deployment models:

items.text: Identity-governed.
An identity provider (IdP) is the ZTA Policy Decision Point. Access is granted based on identity attributes and group membership.
Micro-segmented networks.
Network segmentation is used to restrict access, with software-defined perimeters around individual or groups of resources.
Network infrastructure and software-defined perimeters.
Overlay networks with encrypted tunnels controlled by a trust broker.

runs.text: NIST 800-207 is available free at csrc.nist.gov. The companion document NIST SP 800-207A (2023) addresses ZTA for multi-cloud environments and extends the deployment guidance.

NIST SP 800-207 gives Zero Trust its official definition: verify everything, give the minimum access needed, and design assuming someone is already inside. It's the government's vendor-neutral blueprint for building ZTA.

cards.title: The Seven Pillars of ZTA
cards.teaser: CISA's ZTA maturity model organizes Zero Trust across seven pillars: identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data, automation and orchestration, and visibility and analytics. Each pillar has a maturity trajectory from traditional to optimal.

runs.text: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published the Zero Trust Maturity Model (ZTMM) to provide a structured roadmap. The seven pillars span all the enterprise security domains where ZTA principles must be applied:

items.text: Identity.
Every user, service account, and non-human identity must be authenticated using strong methods (MFA, phishing-resistant FIDO2). Identity is the new perimeter.
Devices.
Only managed, compliant devices receive access. Device posture (OS patch level, EDR status, disk encryption, certificate validity) is checked at authorization time.
Networks.
Traffic is micro-segmented and encrypted. East-west traffic between services is restricted by policy, not just ingress/egress. Software-defined networking enables dynamic policy enforcement.
Applications and Workloads.
Applications enforce their own access controls rather than relying on network location. APIs require authentication tokens. Workloads have assigned identities (SPIFFE/SPIRE or cloud IAM roles).
Data.
Data is classified, labeled, and protected with encryption at rest and in transit. Data loss prevention (DLP) policies gate access based on data sensitivity and user context.
Automation and Orchestration.

Policy enforcement is automated. Responses to security events trigger automated remediation — quarantining a device, revoking a token, alerting a SOC. Manual approvals are reserved for high-stakes decisions.
Visibility and Analytics.
Comprehensive logging and monitoring across all pillars. Behavioral baselines established; anomalies trigger alerts. SIEM and UEBA integrated. You cannot enforce what you cannot see.

runs.text: CISA's ZTMM v2.0 (2023) defines four maturity stages for each pillar: Traditional, Initial, Advanced, and Optimal. Most organizations are at Traditional or Initial across most pillars. The model helps prioritize investment.

ZTA's seven pillars are the seven areas you have to secure: who you are, what device you're on, what network you're using, which app you need, what data you're touching, how responses are automated, and how well you can see what's happening.

cards.title: Perimeter Security vs Zero Trust — The Architecture Shift
cards.teaser: Perimeter security places trust inside a network boundary. Zero Trust eliminates the boundary as a trust signal entirely. The shift is not incremental — it requires redesigning how access decisions are made at every layer.

runs.text: The architectural contrast between perimeter and Zero Trust models:

explanation.code:
PERIMETER MODEL
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TRUSTED INTERNAL NETWORK                           │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐          │
│  │ Server A │  │ Server B │  │   DB     │          │
│  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘          │
│         (unrestricted lateral movement)             │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                       │ Firewall / VPN
              UNTRUSTED INTERNET

ZERO TRUST MODEL
           UNTRUSTED NETWORK (internet or corporate LAN)
  User ──► [Identity + Device Check]
             │
             ▼
    ┌─────────────────┐
    │ Policy Engine   │  ← evaluates every request
    │ (IdP + Context) │
    └────────┬────────┘
             │  Grant / Deny per-resource
             ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   │  App A   │  App B  │  DB    │  (each independently
   │  (auth)  │  (auth) │ (auth) │   enforces policy)
   └──────────────────────────────┘
         (no implicit lateral access)

runs.text: Key architectural differences:

items.text: Trust anchor.
Perimeter: network location. Zero Trust: verified identity + device posture.
Lateral movement.
Perimeter: largely unrestricted once inside. Zero Trust: blocked by default; policy must explicitly allow each service-to-service path.
VPN.
Perimeter: VPN provides broad network access. Zero Trust: no VPN; access proxy provides per-application access.
Breach impact.
Perimeter: one credential breach can expose the whole network. Zero Trust: one credential breach exposes only what that identity was authorized to access.

runs.text: The 2020 SolarWinds breach illustrated the perimeter model's failure mode: attackers with valid credentials moved laterally for months before detection. A mature ZTA with micro-segmentation and continuous verification would have constrained the blast radius significantly.

Old security is a castle moat: hard outside, soft inside. Zero Trust removes the soft inside — every door inside the castle also requires a key, and you only get a key to the rooms you specifically need.

cards.title: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) — Pre-Auth at the Edge
cards.teaser: An Identity-Aware Proxy sits in front of applications and intercepts every request before it reaches the app. It authenticates the user, checks device posture, evaluates access policy, and only proxies requests that pass all checks — making VPNs unnecessary for application access.

runs.text: Google Cloud's Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) and Cloudflare Access are the two leading IAP implementations. Both operate on the same principle: move the authentication and authorization gate from inside the application to a proxy in front of it.
How an IAP works:

items.text: Request interception.
The IAP receives all traffic destined for the application. The application's network endpoint is not publicly exposed — only the IAP's endpoint is.
Identity verification.
The IAP redirects unauthenticated requests to the IdP (Google Workspace, Okta, Azure AD). After authentication, the user's identity token is validated.
Policy evaluation.
The IAP checks whether this identity is permitted to access this resource. Policies can incorporate user groups, device posture (via endpoint verification), location, time of day, and risk score.
Context propagation.
The IAP forwards the authenticated request to the application with signed identity headers (e.g.,
X-Goog-Authenticated-User-Email
for Google IAP). The application can trust these headers without performing its own OAuth flow.

runs.text: Cloudflare Access adds the concept of
service tokens
for non-human clients (CI/CD pipelines, scripts) and
short-lived certificates
for SSH/RDP access — replacing long-lived credentials with ephemeral, auditable access grants.
IAPs are the practical BeyondCorp pattern for organizations that cannot rewrite all their applications. The application does not need to be Zero Trust-aware — the IAP enforces ZTA in front of it.

An Identity-Aware Proxy is a security guard that stands at the door of every application: you log in to the guard, the guard checks your clearance, and only then does it let your request through to the app itself. The app never sees unauthenticated traffic.

cards.title: Mutual TLS (mTLS) — Service-to-Service Identity
cards.teaser: Standard TLS authenticates the server to the client. Mutual TLS (mTLS) adds the reverse — the client also presents a certificate, proving its identity to the server. In a ZTA, mTLS is how services authenticate each other without passwords or API keys.

runs.text: In standard HTTPS, the TLS handshake authenticates only the server (the client verifies the server's certificate). Mutual TLS extends the handshake so both parties present certificates:

items.text: Client certificate.
Each service (or device) holds a certificate issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA), typically an internal CA. The certificate encodes the service's identity (e.g., SPIFFE ID:
spiffe://cluster.local/ns/payments/sa/payment-svc
Handshake verification.
During the TLS handshake, the server requests a client certificate. The client presents it. Both sides verify the other's certificate against the trusted CA chain.
Connection established.
Once mutual verification succeeds, the connection is encrypted and both endpoints are cryptographically authenticated. No API keys or tokens are exchanged in the application layer.

runs.text: mTLS eliminates an entire class of credential-based attacks. There are no passwords to phish, no API keys to leak in environment variables, no JWTs to forge if the signing key is compromised. The certificate private key never leaves the service's memory.
Operational challenges of mTLS at scale:

items.text: Certificate lifecycle management.
Certificates must be issued, rotated, and revoked automatically. Manual certificate management at hundreds of services does not scale. SPIRE (the SPIFFE runtime environment) automates this.
Root CA trust distribution.
All services must trust the same root CA. This requires a PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) that is consistently maintained across the environment.
Certificate revocation.
When a service is compromised, its certificate must be revoked quickly. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) or short-lived certificates (renewed every 24 hours) address this.

runs.text: Normal TLS is like a website showing its ID. mTLS means both sides show ID: the server and the client both prove who they are using certificates. No passwords needed — the certificate is the identity.

cards.title: Service Mesh as ZTA — Istio and Linkerd
cards.teaser: A service mesh injects a sidecar proxy alongside every service. The sidecar handles mTLS, enforces authorization policies, and emits telemetry — without any changes to application code. Istio and Linkerd are the two dominant implementations.

runs.text: A service mesh provides a Zero Trust data plane for microservices. Instead of building mTLS and access control into every service, the mesh offloads this to proxy sidecars that are automatically injected and managed.
Istio architecture:

items.text: Control plane (istiod).
Manages configuration distribution, certificate issuance (via its built-in CA), and service discovery. Issues SPIFFE-compatible certificates to each workload.
Data plane (Envoy sidecars).
An Envoy proxy runs alongside each service pod. All inbound and outbound traffic flows through the sidecar. The sidecar enforces mTLS and authorization policies transparently.
AuthorizationPolicy.
Istio's
AuthorizationPolicy
CRD defines which service identities can call which other services on which ports and paths. This is the ZTA policy in action: every service-to-service call requires explicit policy authorization.

runs.text: Linkerd is a lighter-weight alternative to Istio. It uses a Rust-based micro-proxy (linkerd2-proxy) instead of Envoy, has lower CPU and memory overhead, and focuses on the core features: mTLS, load balancing, observability. Linkerd's simpler model makes it easier to operate.
Both meshes enable a key ZTA pattern:
deny-by-default
. With no
AuthorizationPolicy

applied, Istio in strict mTLS mode still requires all traffic to be mutually authenticated. You can add an explicit deny-all policy and then grant only the paths your architecture requires — achieving micro-segmentation at the application layer.

Istio's PeerAuthentication resource controls the mTLS mode (STRICT, PERMISSIVE, DISABLE) per namespace or workload. Starting in PERMISSIVE mode allows gradual adoption — non-mesh clients still work while mesh clients use mTLS.

A service mesh automatically adds a security proxy next to every microservice. That proxy handles mTLS and checks who is allowed to talk to whom — so every service call is authenticated and authorized without the developer writing a line of security code.

cards.title: Micro-Segmentation — Restricting East-West Traffic
cards.teaser: Micro-segmentation divides the network into small zones with explicit allow-lists between them. It limits lateral movement: even if an attacker compromises one service or host, they cannot reach other resources without matching a policy.

runs.text: Traditional network segmentation puts resources in VLANs or subnets and controls north-south traffic (internet to data center) with firewalls. East-west traffic — between services within the data center — was largely unrestricted. Micro-segmentation closes this gap.
Micro-segmentation approaches:

items.text: Host-based firewalls.
iptables or nftables rules on each host restrict which IP:port combinations can receive connections. Effective but complex to manage at scale without automation.
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy.
Kubernetes
NetworkPolicy
resources define which pods can communicate, using label selectors. Enforced by the CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Weave). A default-deny policy plus explicit allows is the ZTA posture.
Service mesh authorization.
As covered in the service mesh card: Istio/Linkerd AuthorizationPolicies operate at Layer 7, allowing path-level and method-level restrictions that NetworkPolicy (Layer 4) cannot express.
Software-Defined Networking (SDN).
VMware NSX-T, Cisco ACI, and similar SDN platforms enforce micro-segmentation at the hypervisor layer, segmenting even VMs on the same physical host.

runs.text: The practical challenge is discovering the required communication graph before applying policies. Tools like Cilium's Hubble, Istio's Kiali, and AWS VPC Flow Logs help map actual traffic patterns before converting them to explicit allow-lists.

Applying a deny-all micro-segmentation policy without first mapping legitimate traffic will break your applications. Always start in observe/audit mode, build the allow-list from observed traffic, then enforce. The most common ZTA rollout failure is skipping the discovery phase.

Micro-segmentation is putting walls inside your network, not just around it. Each service can only talk to the specific services it needs to, so a compromised service can't freely explore and attack everything else.

cards.title: Continuous Verification — Re-Evaluating Trust on Every Request
cards.teaser: In a Zero Trust model, authentication is not a one-time gate at login. Trust is re-evaluated continuously — on every request, in near real-time — using current identity, device posture, behavioral signals, and risk scores.

runs.text: Traditional access control grants access at login and maintains a session for hours or days. Zero Trust replaces the session model with continuous evaluation: each request carries enough context for the Policy Decision Point to make a fresh access decision.
Signals used in continuous verification:

items.text: Identity freshness.
Short-lived access tokens (JWT expiry of 15 minutes, not 8 hours) force frequent re-authentication. If a token is stolen, its utility window is narrow.
Device posture reassessment.
Device compliance is checked not just at login but continuously. If a device's EDR detects malware between requests, the device loses compliance and access is revoked — even for active sessions.
Behavioral anomaly detection.

UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) establishes baselines. Access at unusual hours, from unusual locations, or to unusual resources raises the risk score and triggers step-up authentication or access denial.
Conditional access policies.
Platforms like Azure AD Conditional Access, Okta's adaptive MFA, and Google BeyondCorp Enterprise evaluate risk signals on every authentication event, not just at session start.

runs.text: The NIST 800-207 Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) and Policy Decision Point (PDP) architecture supports this model. The PEP intercepts every request and asks the PDP for an access decision. The PDP queries the policy engine and current trust signals. The decision is always fresh.

Continuous verification does not mean re-authenticating the user on every HTTP request — that would be unusable. It means the policy engine continuously evaluates device and identity signals in the background, and can revoke access mid-session when signals indicate elevated risk.

Continuous verification means you don't just check someone's ID at the door and let them roam freely. The system keeps watching — if something looks wrong (suspicious behavior, non-compliant device) it can revoke access immediately, even mid-session.

cards.title: Device Posture — Endpoint Health as an Access Signal
cards.teaser: Zero Trust access decisions incorporate the health of the device making the request. A managed, fully patched, EDR-protected device on a compliant configuration receives different access than an unmanaged personal device — or no access at all.

runs.text: Device posture is the set of security attributes a device must satisfy to be considered trustworthy. In the BeyondCorp model, device trust is separate from user trust: even a legitimate user on a compromised device can be denied access.
Typical device posture checks:

items.text: Managed device verification.
Is the device enrolled in MDM (Mobile Device Management) or UEM (Unified Endpoint Management)? Does it have a valid device certificate issued by the corporate CA?
OS and patch level.
Is the operating system within the supported version range? Are critical security patches applied? Access can be blocked or stepped down if the OS is out of date.
Security software.
Is an EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) agent running and reporting clean? Is disk encryption enabled (FileVault, BitLocker)? Is the screen lock configured?
Jailbreak / rooting detection.
Mobile devices that have been jailbroken or rooted have bypassed OS security controls and should not receive access to sensitive corporate resources.

runs.text: Implementation mechanisms:

items.text: Google BeyondCorp Enterprise / Chrome Device Trust.
Device posture signals are passed as attributes in the Chrome browser's context. IAP policies can require specific device posture levels.
Cloudflare Access + WARP client.
The Cloudflare WARP agent on endpoints reports posture signals. Access policies can require specific device checks.
Okta Device Trust / Jamf / Intune.
MDM platforms attest device compliance. The IdP queries the MDM at authentication time and includes device trust in the access decision.

runs.text: Device posture is checking the health of the device, not just the person using it. A legitimate employee on a laptop with unpatched malware is still a security risk. Zero Trust uses the device's health report as part of the access decision.

cards.title: ZTNA — Zero Trust Network Access (VPN Replacement)
cards.teaser: Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) replaces the VPN with per-application, identity-based access. Instead of granting broad network access, ZTNA grants access to specific applications based on verified identity and device posture — reducing attack surface dramatically.

runs.text: VPNs were the enterprise standard for remote access, but they have fundamental ZTA incompatibilities:

items.text: VPN grants network access, not application access.
A VPN-connected user can typically scan and reach any host on the internal network, not just the specific application they need.
VPN does not assess device posture.
A compromised device with valid VPN credentials gets the same access as a clean managed device.
VPN is a binary gate.
Once through, access is static. Context changes (user location, risk score, device posture change) do not affect the active session.

runs.text: ZTNA replaces this with an application-aware, identity-first model:

items.text: No implicit network access.
Users access specific applications through an encrypted tunnel to the ZTNA broker. They have no IP-level visibility into other hosts.
Application connectors.
A lightweight connector runs inside the private network next to each application. It maintains an outbound connection to the ZTNA cloud broker. No inbound firewall ports need to be opened.
Continuous policy enforcement.
Access decisions are re-evaluated continuously. If device posture degrades mid-session, the ZTNA broker can terminate access without waiting for session expiry.

runs.text: Leading ZTNA providers: Cloudflare Access, Zscaler Private Access (ZPA), Palo Alto Prisma Access, Google BeyondCorp Enterprise, Cisco Duo. Most are cloud-delivered SASE components.

Gartner predicts ZTNA as the dominant enterprise remote access technology by 2025, replacing legacy VPN. The shift is driven by cloud adoption, remote work normalization, and the fundamental VPN architectural mismatch with Zero Trust principles.

A VPN puts you inside the network — from there you can reach many things. ZTNA puts you in front of exactly one application at a time, and only if you pass the identity and device check. It's the difference between a building passkey and a room-by-room badge system.

cards.title: SASE — Converged Network and Security as a Service
cards.teaser: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) converges SD-WAN, ZTNA, CASB, SWG, and FWaaS into a single cloud-delivered service. Gartner introduced the term in 2019 to describe the architectural direction that eliminates point security products in favor of unified, identity-driven, cloud-native security.

runs.text: Gartner analysts Neil MacDonald and Joe Skorupa coined SASE (pronounced "sassy") in their 2019 report "The Future of Network Security Is in the Cloud." It describes the convergence of:

items.text: SD-WAN (Software-Defined Wide Area Network).
Intelligent traffic routing between branch offices, data centers, and cloud providers. Replaces MPLS with internet-based connectivity optimized for cloud applications.
ZTNA.
Zero Trust remote access for users, as described in the previous card.
CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker).
Visibility and control over SaaS application usage. Enforces data security policies, detects shadow IT, and prevents data exfiltration through cloud apps.
SWG (Secure Web Gateway).
Filters web traffic, blocks malicious sites, enforces acceptable-use policies. Cloud-delivered — no on-premise proxy appliance.
FWaaS (Firewall as a Service).
Next-generation firewall capabilities delivered from the cloud. Inspects traffic across all ports and protocols, not just HTTP/HTTPS.

runs.text: The key SASE property: security enforcement happens at the edge of the cloud network, close to the user, regardless of where the user is or where the application runs. The corporate data center is no longer the traffic hub.

Leading SASE vendors: Cloudflare One, Zscaler, Palo Alto Prisma SASE, Cato Networks, Netskope. Each has different strengths in the ZTNA vs. SWG vs. CASB components — most enterprises use a hybrid of 2-3 vendors.

SSE (Security Service Edge) is the security-only subset of SASE (ZTNA + CASB + SWG), without the SD-WAN networking component. Many organizations adopt SSE first — getting the security controls — and add SD-WAN separately. Gartner defined SSE in 2021.

SASE is the idea that your network and security infrastructure should be one cloud service, not a pile of separate boxes. Instead of routing all traffic back to headquarters to be inspected, SASE inspects and secures traffic at the cloud edge, wherever the user happens to be.

cards.title: Implementing ZTA — A Practical Migration Roadmap
cards.teaser: Zero Trust is not a switch you flip — it is a multi-year architectural transformation. The practical path starts with identity consolidation, adds device posture, progresses to application-level access control, and completes with full micro-segmentation and continuous verification.

runs.text: Organizations that attempt to implement ZTA all at once fail. The practical approach is incremental, moving through maturity stages while maintaining operational stability. The CISA ZTMM phases align with this progression:

items.text: Phase 1: Identity foundation.

Consolidate identity into a single IdP. Enforce MFA universally — particularly phishing-resistant FIDO2/passkeys for privileged accounts. Eliminate shared credentials and service accounts with long-lived passwords. This single phase blocks the majority of breaches.
Phase 2: Device visibility and posture.
Deploy MDM/UEM. Inventory all devices. Issue device certificates. Begin blocking unmanaged devices from accessing sensitive applications. Deploy EDR on all managed devices.
Phase 3: Application-level access control.
Deploy an IAP (Google IAP, Cloudflare Access) in front of sensitive internal applications. Replace VPN remote access with ZTNA. Enforce least-privilege access policies per application.
Phase 4: Service-to-service ZTA.
Deploy a service mesh with mTLS. Define explicit AuthorizationPolicies for service-to-service communication. Implement micro-segmentation with Kubernetes NetworkPolicy or SDN.
Phase 5: Continuous verification and analytics.

Integrate SIEM/UEBA. Establish behavioral baselines. Configure adaptive access policies that increase authentication requirements when risk scores elevate. Close the feedback loop between security monitoring and access control.

runs.text: The most common ZTA failure mode is purchasing a ZTNA or SASE product without addressing identity first. The platform enforces access based on identity — if identity hygiene is poor (shared accounts, no MFA, excessive permissions) the ZTA controls are built on sand.

ZTA migration is a five-phase journey: first get identity right (SSO + MFA), then know your devices, then control app access, then secure service-to-service calls, then add continuous monitoring. Skip the identity foundation and everything else is fragile.

cards.title: Least-Privilege Identity — Just-in-Time Access
cards.teaser: Least-privilege identity in a ZTA context means eliminating standing privileged access in favor of just-in-time (JIT) grants, time-bounded credentials, and ephemeral roles. Permanent admin access is itself a vulnerability — it just hasn't been exploited yet.

runs.text: Standing access — permanent membership in powerful groups like
admins
or
database-owners

— is a latent risk. If the account is compromised, the attacker has persistent elevated access. JIT access eliminates standing privilege by granting elevated permissions only when needed, only for the duration needed.
JIT access patterns:

items.text: Privileged Access Management (PAM).

Tools like CyberArk, HashiCorp Vault, and BeyondTrust mediate privileged access. A developer requests SSH access to a production server; the PAM system verifies identity + manager approval, issues a time-limited SSH certificate (valid for 4 hours), and logs every session.
Cloud IAM ephemeral roles.

AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly SSO), Azure PIM (Privileged Identity Management), and GCP's IAM Conditions allow time-bound role assignments. A user activates a role for a specific maintenance window; it expires automatically.
Workload identity federation.

CI/CD pipelines and services obtain short-lived credentials via OIDC federation rather than storing long-lived AWS Access Keys or service account keys. GitHub Actions, for example, can authenticate to AWS using a token valid for 15 minutes via OIDC.
Secrets management.
HashiCorp Vault issues dynamic secrets (database passwords, cloud credentials) that are generated for each request and expire after a configurable TTL. No static password to leak or rotate.

runs.text: The ZTA principle: every identity — human or non-human — should have exactly the permissions required for its current task, granted for the minimum duration required, with full audit logging of every exercise of that access.

HashiCorp Vault's secret lease model is a practical implementation of JIT least-privilege for non-human identities. Leases are renewable but never permanent. When a workload is decommissioned, its leases expire automatically — no cleanup step required.

Least-privilege identity means nobody has permanent admin access — instead, you request elevated permissions for a specific task, get them for an hour, use them, and they expire. A stolen credential only gives an attacker a narrow window, not a permanent skeleton key.
